title: Lot's of Technology employed to cook but boy does it cook.
text:
Let me start by saying that I take online reviews seriously as it’s a major factor in my decision making process. That being said, I also am weary of items that have too many 5-Star ratings. Fake reviews are usually pretty easy to spot as they lack the detail of a real user.

I can assure you I am a real user…

I had not considered Induction cooking until we had a power outage. I know, strange way to lead into this but it’s my review and that’s where I’m starting.. Anyway, I was away on business when our home lost power and while the wife and kids were able to manage the small generator we use (3000 Watt) there was no way for here to cook other than the Microwave. Solution: induction hot plate. I love to cook so when it came in the mail I was excited to try it out and boy was I impressed with what it could do. So much so that it was our Go-To item for cooking one pot meals. This is how I ended up searching for an Induction range to replace my 20+ year old Jenn-Air which was the style with the center downdraft and changeable cartridges. At $2000 back in the day, you could say I loved to cook then as much as I do now.

On to the GE…

I’m typically “Frugal” and this purchase was no exception. I bought it from a supplier on the East Coast as a scratch and dent and saved almost $1500. It had a few issues that were easily addressed by me and for all intent and purpose, it’s brand new. I ended up with this model as it is one of only a few double oven induction stoves on the market that were in my price range. Why 2 ovens? Holidays and 2 boys that love pizza rolls and junk food that tastes better cooked in an oven but don’t need to heat up a full size oven (Toaster oven is not an option thanks…). That’s pretty much how I ended up with the GE, Induction, price, and double oven. Not a lot to choose from for me in my search.

First off, this thing is a tank. VERY heavy compared to my Jenn-Air. Removing the Jenn was a one man (me) job but I had to enlist the help of my 15 year old for the GE. Not an issue just a note. Other than that it slid in as any range would. I was able to remove the feet from my Jenn to make it flush with the counter top, not this unit. I was afraid removing the leveling feet would not allow for the bottom oven to open properly as it’s very close to the ground.

The top oven is just big enough with 2 rack positions for casseroles and general use with smaller items. I baked Stuffed Shells and Sauce last night with no issues at all. The rack in the lower position is a little tricky pulling out to get to your meal with oven mitts on but after time you get used to it as best you can. I usually have a spatula or spoon handy to assist in pulling it out.

The bottom oven is smaller than I’m used to (duh…) but have not run into anything that won’t fit yet. Unfortunately it arrived 5 days after Thanksgiving so I was not able to test with a “bagged” 18lb Turkey. They are still on sale so I’ll try to sneak one in next week once the family is over me making some form of Turkey for dinner for 2 weeks straight. The convection is “true” convection which means it has its own heating element around the fan which you can see glow as the oven running. I do not believe the Jenn had this feature. So far I have not cooked anything that would test this other than Calzones and they browned nicely.

The bottom oven required “calibration” which is easy to do. Just buy an oven thermometer and if the oven is at 350 and the thermometer is reading 340 add 10 degrees. Nice feature however the day I pulled the Jenn out it was within one degree. What did surprise me was that the bottom oven needed calibration to the tune of +15 degrees?? Maybe something to do with the scratch –n- dent but as long as I have the ability to dial it in I’m ok with the savings. Note that it also has a self adjust feature that takes into account convection and it lowers the temp a bit. I have not tested this and currently have it turned off as I like to have full control. Back to calibrating, I let both sit at temp (400 degrees) for 15 minutes after it said they were at temp to make sure they had settled in on temp before adjusting. As for Pre-heating… GE is a little optimistic on the amount of time it takes to preheat as neither oven is truly at temp for another 5 minutes after the stove say’s “Pre-Heat Complete” according to my test thermometer. I have not tried to cook when it tells me that the oven is ready as I know that it’s typically at least 15% less than my setpoint. The good news is that we had another power outage and the oven held the offset I put in for the bottom oven.

Induction… What can I say… I absolutely love what this stove can do. The large burner will boil a couple of gallons of water for spaghetti in no time and to the point where if left on high it will splash on the microwave installed over the range, it’s that vigorous of a boil! Then when you turn it off, it stops… No residual heat that continues the boil long after you turn off the element forcing you to move the pot to an unplanned emergency location. I can boil pasta in a large pot at medium with this thing after it comes to the initial boil! To me, this is the future of cooking and will potentially eliminate the need for a gas stove for the home Chef. The control is amazing enough that even the casual user will note that you can easily and quickly find the setting that simmers without cooling off or eventually boiling. To test this, try cooking Minute Tapioca (love the stuff). With the Jenn, I always had scalded egg at the bottom of the pot as I would get impatient and bring it to a boil on not medium but medium high (while whisking). With the GE, it boiled at medium (5 on the knob) in no time at all and there was no scalded egg residue on the bottom of the pan and simple rinsing cleaned the pot (no scrubbing). Those of you that “cook” will understand what I’m talking about. I have not tried bridging the 2 elements together as I currently do not have the cookware to take advantage of this. As my Jenn allowed me to “grill” indoors, I will be looking for a grill and griddle for this very feature.

Precision cooking? Have not used it to cook, only test to see if it works. Word of caution on this however if you are cooking delicate stuff. If you start out cold and set the temp to say 180 degrees, the stove will go full throttle to get it to temp which could mean scalded sauce on the bottom of your pan. It also will over shoot pretty badly doing this as well. My testing suggests getting it close to the temp you want, then turn the feature on and it will hold that temp until you tell it otherwise or whatever you are cooking evaporates and you ruin your pot or the auto shutoff kicks in!

Not sure why they put the Warmer on the stovetop. The control over the burners is so good there is really no need for it unless you trying to juggle 5 pans on the top.

I’ve noticed as many reviewers have stated that some pots are noisier than others. I’ve also noticed that the amount of “buzz” seems to relate to the quality of the pot. Good heavy ones do not make much if any noise. Cheaper “thin/light” pots will buzz noticeably but not a deal breaker for me.

The oven controls take some getting used to as they seem overly complicated. Not that you won’t be able to figure them out easily enough but there are a few more button presses to turn on the oven that I’m used to with the Jenn. Example of the bottom oven button sequence: Bottom Oven, Convect, 350, start. With the Jenn, Convect, 350. It would realize you were done and set the temp to 350 without having to press another button. Not a big deal but takes some getting used to. They have quick functions like Pizza, Frozen Food, etc. but they are all set for 350?? When was the last time you cooked a pizza of any sort at 350?? (Again those that cook will get it.) I’m assuming this can be changed but I have yet to open the manual (did I mention I’m a 50 year old Controls Engineer by trade? :-) ) I also discovered that cleaning the stove top while baking is not advised. The touch pad appears to be capacitive and when touched by a wet rag will inevitably change the oven setting and once it thinks you are wanting to change something by touching the key pad if you don’t complete the button sequence it will turn the oven off… Good thing I heard the beeps as I was cleaning up and noticed the upper oven was accidentally turned off with my dinner in it! Just note that it’s very sensitive to a flopping wet rag… (you can lock the controls to keep this from happening as well). This is the first smooth top range I’ve owned and I’m already seeing the benefits and ease of cleaning. There were a few times I thought the Health Department was going to shut me down on the Jenn as it has so many nooks and crannies.

The knobs for the elements are heavily weighted and I like that. They feel professional.

It was easy to set up WiFi. I have the app and can control and get notifications. I can also tell Alexa to “Tell Geniva to preheat the top oven to 350 degrees” and it will turn on (after Alexa verifies that’s what I want to do first). More of a party trick than anything as by the time I remember what to say I could have walked over and turned it on. Do I need this? No. Do I wish manufactures would stop with this nonsense? YES!!!

Another thing to note is the vents on the back of the stove top. These are for the ovens and the cooking elements (Cooling air flow). I have no issues with them other than the holes are rather large and I can see myself dropping food down them as I tend to pretend I’m a Chef by tossing my noodles and sauce rather than stirring it… I think once it goes in, it will be hard to get out. There is also an oddly placed gasket at the top front of the stove where the stainless and glass top meet. It seems to be pretty soft and looks like it could harbor food and other “stuff”. It’s easily disrupted by cleaning (as in it moves a bit) and just does not feel quite right. I would rather see a harder rubber piece in this location.

In short (lol… Word is saying I’m close to 2000 words!!), I love Induction. So much so that this will be the only type of stove I buy moving forward! The oven is well.. an oven. It’s an insulated box with a heating element in it. Not sure I see anything as ground breaking as I do Induction. I plan on cooking some bread this weekend and will get more of a feel for how it works then. My biggest fear with this range is the electronics. Between the key pad, internet, and induction it has an awful lot of technology being employed to simply boil some water but boy does it ever boil water!! I just hope it lasts as long as the Jenn (which still works perfectly btw…).

If GE happens to read this… Scale back on the Tech, turn the warmer into another cooking element, add one timer for each oven (only a single timer? My Jenn had 2 with only one oven!), and add a timer to at least one cook top burner that would turn the burner off at the end of the timer!! That would be basically a built in "Insta-Pot"

Thanks for bearing with me!

12/27/2018 Update:

Cooked a 16lb Turkey today and had no issues. As you can see the bag is close to the top of the oven but didn't expand and touch the element or oven ceiling. The bottom rack has a nice drawer slide that makes pulling out to access pretty easy. I must say I don't care much for having to stoop all the way down to get to the bottom oven but there really is no other alternative if you don't have the room for wall mounted ovens. I'll live with it.
So far I am very impressed with the oven and have had no issues (or regrets)!

title: A little slice of heaven right here on earth
text:
We moved into a new home that made it impossible to run a water line to the fridge. As a result we were living day to day with bagged ice from a nearby store (we now live in the country, so its bigger deal than it sounds). It became clear that we were looking at moving back to tray ice or buying an ice machine.

I was close to pulling the trigger on a light-duty commercial ice machine when I found several sites recommending this surface unit and we couldn't be happier. It creates soft, chewable ice in a very reasonable amount of time. The unit is rather large and heavy, which is not that big of a deal (it feels solid). Noise wise it hums about as loud as a microwave while creating ice, but when done its completely silent. It creates more ice than three of us can consume (and we're all ice chewers) and adds up pretty quickly. We move unused ice to the ice machine in the freezer and now it too dispenses chewable ice too. It makes so much that I've started bagging it and taking it down to a guest house we have on property for visitors to enjoy as well.

Are we now spoiled? We've caught ourselves looking at the ice when we go out now and say "we have better ice at home". So, yeah.

I connected it to a permanent water line which removes one more step in the process since we keep it on all the time. If you're in the market, note that ice production is slow but consistent - don't purchase one and turn it on an hour before a party and expect ice. There are also some restrictions about moving it and allowing the unit to settle before turning it back on (fridges say the same thing) so while portable, include that into your prep time for ice usage.

Definitely a thumbs up if it's what you're looking for.

title: This washing machine has been awesome. The setup took some trial and error and ...
text:
This washing machine has been awesome. The setup took some trial and error and the instructional booklet didn't provide much help when it came to the errors. Here are a few things to consider before buying this machine or for troubleshooting after purchase:

Pros:
-Fully-automatic (does not require babysitting once you learn the setup)
-Larger-than expected load capacity
-Drain pump that drains the majority of the water left in the machine after wash
-Several wash settings, including Heavy, Normal, and Gentle
-Washes quite rapidly, seemingly just as well as any other washer
-Spin cycle
-Quiet machine

Cons:
-Small hose for drainage (must be in very close proximity to somewhere to drain the water (bathtub, sink, or drain floor)
-Adapter for sink hookup needs to be EXTREMELY tight for automatic water shut-off to work properly and not spray out the sides
-Settings do not really allow you to customize very much
-Sometimes spin cycle is so powerful that it can tear through delicate items (I recommend using a mesh bag)
-Lint filter does very little

Overall, I give it a 5/5. I use it several times a week. The spin cycle brings clothes to just damp and I can usually hang dry after that (with the exception of heavy towels that need to be dried). The castor wheels allow for easy transportation and the machine isn't too heavy. This thing is great for a small apartment, tiny house, or even a regular household on a budget or an individual/family looking for eco-friendly, budget-friendly washing options. Definitely has saved us money already on laundry cost.

We replaced this machine with a brand named Aicok after reading reviews extensively. We have only had it for a few weeks, but the Aicok has many more features (such as a timer) and it holds ice longer due to better insulation. It was about the same price when purchased.

text:
This is citric acid. It’s the same sort of product you use to descale a “fancy” coffee machine. You simply mix it with water and pour it into your countertop ice machine and let it run. Most ice machines have a “clean cycle”, which is where it simply fills and empties. . . over-and-over. . . for about 20-minutes. I use a bottle brush to brush around all of the inside as well. Then you empty. . . rinse. . . and run the machine on the “clean cycle” again. I usually rinse a couple of times.

There’s nothing “wrong” with this product, other than the cost. It’s Made in China and being sold by a Chinese company on Amazon. At the current price of 10 bucks, it’s well over twice the price it should be 3 – 4 bucks would be more appropriate. Even then it would be pricey. If you look online for coffee machine descaler; you’ll find a lot less expensive options.

The cloths do not come out feeling crunchy like a soaking wet towel dried in the sun though, they feel pretty darn soft! Obviously not as soft as a heated dryer but very manageable for a daily wear. My only complaint is the hoses, I’d love them to be just a little bit longer and thicker. But both were long enough. I seriously spent months adding a ton of different brands and styles to my Amazon cart and removing them with fear they would waste money. But I can assure you I wish I had bought this sooner. Excruciating experience with the Bertazzoni service. We bought a Bertazzoni gas range Master 30" a year ago. The week before Easter of this year the oven ignition broke down. It is now mid-May and it has yet to be fixed! They kept saying that the needed part will be mailed overnight to the company servicing the range and that we'll have it fixed over the next couple of days. I just talked to them and was told that the part is back-ordered and they can not do anything about it! Really? It will be 6 weeks by then! After insisting that they get it fixed asap and after being put on hold I am told that they "found" the part. It remains to be seen if indeed we will have a working oven soon...

Now about the performance of this range: first, the range looks good! Second, the top burners are fine especially when you need high heat. My only complaint is that the simmering is not performing well. Even with the simmering ring there is way too much heat for a slow cooking stew in a Dutch oven. My solution: I pile two grates such that the Dutch oven stays high enough. The downside: it looks ridiculous and I can not use the other burners! The oven: works fine for cooking/braising meat which requires more moisture but not so well for baking which can not be turned and therefore gets burnt on the bottom. My solution for this was to place a metal tray underneath such that the heat gets diffused and circulates better (this happens even with the fan on). Bottom line: first, appliances sometimes break down and that is fine but then the service should be of quality and prompt; second, for the price this range should work without these rather embarrassing adjustments! I have made an effort to like this range, hence the adjustments, but the service I have received so far really sealed my thoughts on the Bertazzoni, and they are not positive!

The problem we had was with the enormous depth/ short height of the refrigerator box, low deep shelves, extra forward door thickness, PLUS THE VERY SHARP lower edges of the freezer door handle when the lower door is open. title: Different approach to blocking vents works well
text:
Most covers are magnetic, stick to the front of the vent, and (as one gathers from reviews) don't stay in place very well. They also hide decorative covers in less-than decorative manner. These rubber vent covers fit on the *back* of the vent cover, which means that the air in the ducts helps to hold the cover in place--important if you have a situation like mine, in which the central-air fan occasionally and inexplicably goes into leaf-blower mode.

The covers arrive rolled up and compressed in a small box, and have to be carefully peeled apart. Easing open the folds on a cover is a bit nerve-wracking; none of mine tore, but the inside surfaces were sufficiently stuck that it seemed like a very real possibility. The black rubber is reasonably odorless.

I've deployed two of the three covers, and they are working very well. It will be interesting to see how long they last.

title: THIS MULTI-PURPOSE PORTABLE DRYING/WARMING SYSTEM DOES EXACTLY AS ADVERTISED
text:
I found this versatile multi-purpose portable dryer/warmer product to be exactly as advertised on the product webpage so I am not going to go into a review of all the features in this review. Instead, I will focus on notes and observations and my experience using it. I have attached many pictures which speak for themselves.

Notes:
1) The hanger rack has 5 notches. I put 4 items on it and there was very little room between the items. (see test results below).
2) The heater/fan unit will automatically turn off if the unit tilts completely over - safety - it will not restart itself.
3) The fan will continue after you turn off the heater, when the timer runs down or it fall over. This is for safety - it is cooling off the internal heater.
4) The display panel reflects three items: P1/P2 mode, 3 digit timer or 3 dashes. (see pics). The power button controls the mode and activates the timer to the default of 120 min. The 3 dashes indicates OFF.
5) P1 is used for drying fabrics. P2 is used for blanket, hand or general heat warming as well as shoe drying.
6) +/- buttons adjust the duration from 30m to 360m.
7) The hook can be used on a door or a pole. I used a doorway molding so that I could observe the unit during the test.
8) Probably the most important "prohibition" is do NOT use it near water - such as over a bathtub hanging from a shower rod. An equally important safety rule is do NOT let fabrics brush against the heater/fan unit (158F/70C degrees heat).
9) When using the bag, make sure that the Drip Shield/Heat Reflector is placed above the fan outlet. It catches water drips and diverts them to the side - safety feature. (see pic)
10) The Drip Shield and the Hose Base have 4 strong magnets to hold them in place on the heater/fan.
11) The hose base and blower end screw onto the hose for stability - the hose compresses and expands between 1 foot and almost 3.5 feet. To screw the hose base and blower end onto the hose, the ends need to be compressed for the threads to catch.
12) The shoe dryer fits over the end of the hose blower end piece.
13) If you set the heater/fan on the floor, it must be a hard floor, NOT carpeting. The base of the unit has very tiny "feet" to allow air to flow into the bottom of the unit. That air input must not be blocked.

Warranty:
Neither the product webpage or the Instruction Manual identify the warranty and neither give seller contact information - phone number or home webpage. I managed to trace the warranty for this item via AMAZON seller links and discovered "An zhong is committed to providing each customer with the highest standard of customer service". Your only method of contacting them is via the AMAZON seller (An zhong) contact tool.

Test:
I ran a load of wash with medium spin - wet but not dripping. I selected 1 towel, 1 sweatshirt, 1 T-shirt and 1 flannel pajama bottom and used sturdy plastic hangers. (I was concerned about the plastic hangers melting but they worked fine - there are no restrictions documented about what type of hangers to use: metal, wood or plastic.) I used the default P1 drying mode and 120 min duration. The unit functioned perfectly.

Results:
The bag is not very deep so the 4 items I tested were close together (touching). The lower and upper portions of all the items were dry. The two items on the outside (towel and T-shirt) were dry on the outside (near bag wall) but they were slightly damp on the inside. The middle sweatshirt and flannel pajama bottom were damper but definitely nowhere near as wet as at the beginning. This is not a defect - additional timing finished the drying job nicely - I added 1 more hour.

The heat right out of the heater/fan unit was too hot to hold my hand in it for more than a few seconds (see safety note above). The heat coming out of the top vents was warm and did not burn.

Oddities:
1) Webpage says this unit can be used while camping outdoors - you would need a 110-120v 60hz generator or hookup which can support 600w, otherwise, I can't see how it would work.
2) On the same page in the Instruction Manual it refers to 110-120v 60hz as well as 110-/50hz. AC. The unit itself says 110-/60hz. 60hz is used in N America, parts of central and south America. Most of the rest of the world uses 50hz. FYI
3) The Instruction Manual needs a translation for the translation - much of the text was a head-scratcher and pretty amusing. I suggest that you just use common sense in the assembly and use. It has many "thou shalt nots" that you should try to figure out.

title: Is the flow rate loss worth the savings?
text:
The important things on a filter and the level of filtration and flow rate. This hits the first pretty well, as its both NSF 42 and 53 compliant (many third party filters are *not* NSF53 certified). Briefly, NSF42 is taste/odor (chlorine etc.) which is about the least you'd expect a filter to do. NSF 53 reduces things like lead and VOC, so that's really an important check. It doesn't have NSF 401 (which the OEM does), which handles other contaminants like pesticides and pharmaceuticals, so it's still not quite as good of a filter. (In fairness, the Waterdrop Plus does offer 401 filtering).

The second mark is flow rate. This isn't bad per se, but it is noticeably slower than the OEM model.

So the question is do you care about NFS401 filtering and do you mind waiting a bit longer to fill your cup if it saves you a few bucks? Personally I'll probably go back to OEM and I use it to fill my coffee pot and the flow rate is a big ask for me, but that may not be the case for everyone.

title: It has operated fine for me
text:
I have owned this model for 10 months. It has operated fine for me. I only use the timed setting, but there are also options for Permanent Press and Cottons. 60 minutes gets clothes dry, but you can run it up to 80 for larger/thicker loads.

I never wash extra large loads of clothes, so I'd probably be safe putting two washer loads in this dryer at the same time without exceeding the rating. My washing machine is only designed to handle 3.9 Cu. Ft., and this dryer is rated at 6.8 Cu. Ft.

The nicest feature of this dryer is the light inside the tub that is triggered to come on when I open the door. A light is such a simple, but thoughtful addition. That extra illumination ensures I don't leave a sock or some other small article of clothing behind.

The biggest design flaw of this dryer is location of the lint filter. It's positioned just below the access to the tub with no screen between the filter and the door. Whenever I open the door, the suction from the door causes bits of loose lint to come flying out all over the floor. Thankfully, I have a separate wash room. If this dryer was in a hallway, I'd need to vacuum after every load to keep the lint from getting all over the house. Having the filter inside the door like that might be a good reminder to clean out the lint after every load, but that's about the only advantage. If I were buying a dryer today, I'd go with another model due to this particular flaw in the design.

I purchased this dryer from Lowes when they had it on sale for $399. I bought the extended 3-year warranty, so the total was approximately $460. This model is currently priced $440 at Lowes without the warranty.

UPDATE 7/31/16: I am updating this review and reducing the rating from 3-stars to 2-stars. I have now owned this dryer for two years. About six months ago, the On switch became finicky and would not start the dryer. I finally figured out I can get it to start if I twist the button counterclockwise. I will be calling Lowes to see if they will repair this problem under the extended warranty I purchased at some point. All in all, my impression of this dryer is that it's not the greatest design, and the parts are cheap.

title: Excellent features but started to have issues with this product ...
text:
Excellent features but started to have issues with this product short after I bought it brand new with my house. Three months after moving to the house, the ice dispenser started clogging every once in a while, but it became more frequent as time passed. I now have to take out and shake the ice tray every week or so to get the ice flowing again. I use the ice dispenser every day.

About three months after the ice dispenser started clogging, the fridge started leaking on the floor just a few drops a day. I noticed a small water spot under the front left corner. Not a biggie for me as I just wipe it off every three days or so when it became really noticeable.

But a year later, the control panel started showing an “F1” error code, and the water and ice dispensers stopped working. I called LG US Customer Service and I was told that this is a known issue with the ‘freezer fan’. They told me to disconnect the unit for about 3 -4 hours to allow the fan to “unfreeze”, and that would clear the issue. I tried that three times and the error came back every time. After researching in the internet I found that several customers have had the same exact issues with this unit, to the extent that there is a Class Action law suit ongoing. Unfortunately, LG Customer Care is now saying my unit is out of warranty. So I paid $2000 for that unit with the house and a year and a half later I might have to come out of pocket for repairs. I have filled out the Claim Form for repair coverage as part of the Class Action lawsuit in hopes that LG will honor their product quality. But for now, I can’t recommend nor give a descent rating for this product. I will update my review once I hear back from LG and if/when the issues are corrected.

Used a large oversized mug and my “usual” amount of ground coffee (6tbsp of whole beans - hey, it’s a huge mug).

However.. there are a few things I did wrong and few things to be aware of in general with this admittedly very cool filtering straw.

1 - how fine you grind the beans is VERY important. Too fine and the mesh will struggle to filter it, resulting in a strange mouthfeel and actual consumption of ground coffee. I’m limited by my grinder here, which uses blades that pulverize unevenly and produces some fine dust regardless of overall coarseness.

2 - putting too much ground coffee in your cup will choke the filter, so as you suck you’ll notice it becoming harder to drink and you need to stop, swirl the straw, and try again. When you get down to the sludgy bottom, it clogs pretty quick.

3 - maybe this should have been my first point but.. you can’t use boiling water unless you want to burn yourself, or at least you have to let the coffee sit until cool enough to drink, which impacts the strength and flavor tremendously. When camping, you’re probably going to boil water until it’s bubbling.. and then I guess wait for it to cool? Seems like there’s going to be some trial and error involved.

Aside from the above, I think it’s a very clever and mostly well implemented idea. The hardware is well constructed and feels sturdy and will last a while. The fabric drawstring carry case is simple and large enough for a couple straws and the included cleaning brush.

The cup of coffee I prepared was wonderfully strong and rich, far better than any instant you’d usually knock together when camping. And the grinds are biodegradable and easily disposed.

Really love the concept, mostly love the coffee it lets you drink, but you need a decent portable grinder (or pre-ground coffee) of a specific coarseness for this to work as intended I feel.

title: Simple Review
text:
I purchased this washer (and the dryer) in June of 2011 and I will admit to some user error issues initially. It's EXTREMELY good but you have to be diligent with the controls. If you use the settings correctly...you will not fail. If you think you know everything and don't need to read up on it you're not going to like the results.

For instance, I have a lot of embellished t-shirts that I used to just put in my old washer and then air dry. Well, I did that with one of my t-shirts on the normal cycle with max water extraction and it shook a lot of the sequins off it which was upsetting. Now I know I have to use it on the hand wash cycle when washing my embellished t-shirts.

The other thing was that I was used to putting a bit of bleach in the washer when I cleaned my duvet cover which is white with red trim. Well, I did that with the new washer and I ended up needing to shop for a new duvet cover because the trim on the old one got bleached. *sigh*

The washer is super smart in that it ONLY uses as much water as it needs which isn't a lot. It's actually kinda freaky how much water it uses. And you don't have to set the water level...it does it all for you based on how many clothes you've put in. With less water my brain figures the bleach is much more potent so yeah...disaster lesson learned.

The only thing I don't like is that I have to get used to cleaning the machine with Affresh. I've never had to do that before so when the indicator light came on, I was taken aback. I guess it didn't sit too well with me that I had to clean the machine seeing as though in my mind...it gets clean as the clothes are cleaned. Once I ran the clean cycle with Affresh, the light went off. I've only had to do it once so far so maybe the cost for 3 of the Affresh tablets for $9 isn't too bad.

A friend of a friend suggested leaving the top of the washer open between uses in order to have it dry out completely and combat any potential smells which may occur. I have yet to encounter these smells some people talk about but the threat of them showing up definitely made it so that I leave the top open now.

I love this washer and I love the results. I would recommend this set to anyone.

title: Worked Great for a Week/Will be repaired/replaced by GE Service
text:
Purchased and received this cooktop the end of June - it was installed by a licensed electrician in early August. Due to painting in my kitchen, it was under protective covering until a week ago when I was finally able to use it.

I was extremely impressed with its rapid boil and easy to operate controls. I cooked a few meals on it and was extremely happy with it. It cleans easily and is very intuitive to use. The temperature controls are very responsive. Water boils very quickly, and if you turn the temp down, or off, the pot stops boiling IMMEDIATELY. It is as responsive as a gas cooktop, if not more.

I had read some reviews that some of these cooktops have issues where the burner won't stay on and shuts right off. Unfortunately, I am one of the people now experiencing this same problem. I put on a big pot to boil and all was going just fine - the pot was at a rolling boil and I added my pasta to the pot...and it shut off. It would not turn back on. The fan was running and would not shut off either. The 2 burners on the left work perfectly. The two burners on the right have not worked since Saturday (it's now Monday). The fan also never shut off and ran constantly since the burner shut off.

I called GE's service line at 9AM and they had a service technician at my house by 11:30AM. He ran diagnostics on the unit and it seems like it has a bad module, possible loose connections, and possible issues with the user interface (the glass cooktop part with the controls). Replacement parts have been ordered and a return visit has been scheduled for a week from Wednesday to replace the entire unit. In the meantime I still have the use of the left side burners - and I feel confident that the problems are going to be rectified as quickly as possible.

I so far happy with the sense of urgency in which GE service has responded to the issue. It's, of course, under warranty, so it's a minor inconvenience for me at this point to have to wait another 9 days for the stove to be fully functional.

I will say that delivery of the unit was quick, and it arrived in pristine condition - extremely well packaged with no visible sign of any damage. My electrician installed it while I was away on vacation - my contractor did not advise me of any issues with installation.

I do not think that the malfunction is the fault of the seller - I believe it is a known issue with these induction cooktops, and I expect once it is repaired that I will have no future issues - however I will look into an extended service warranty all the same.

Once repaired I expect to go back to being extremely happy with the cooktop.

It did come with a Hestancue saute pan which has a bluetooth compatible sensor that interfaces with both the cooktop and the Hestancue app on my smartphone. I did use it to make pancakes on Saturday morning, and I have to say they were the best I've ever made. The app walks you through the recipe and then cooking steps, and the stove and pan work together to automatically control the temperature of the pan throughout the process. The app is not the easiest to use and the directions/instructions are awkwardly written and could use some massaging from a technical writer--but I managed to get it to work without too much frustration. The app did quit on me several times during the cooking of the individual pancakes - but I muddled through it. Could use improvement - but is functional as is and is a very innovative feature that I do like a lot. I am glad the stovetop came with a pan because the pans themselves are quite costly and I do not think that I would shell out that kind of money for one on my own. It is good to know what the pan can do - and I can decide at another time whether to invest in additional pieces.

I've given this 3 Stars as this was the best price I could find for the unit, and I do LOVE it (when operational). I knew that I might have this problem when I purchased it. I am confident that GE will make things right and they were quick to respond. If I had not had this problem it would be a 5 star review. I believe there was a chance I'd have had this issue no matter where I purchased it.

title: Really nice fridge, but needs redesigns to get 5 stars from me.
text:
We researched quite a bit to find the fridge we wanted. Guess I should have spent a little more time with this one in person.

PROS:
Don't get me wrong...it's a great fridge. The black stainless on this LG is like a high-dollar paint job on a luxury car. Very deep and shiny and does NOT take fingerprints at all like regular stainless. You also can't use magnets on it. So no matter how many sticky-fingered kids you have in your house, this fridge will look like brand new for a long time.

There is tons of room in the fridge portion and the adjustable everything makes it easy to customize the interior for your organizational style (we all have one...milk and juice on the upper right, condiments in the door, beer and sodas on the left). Many options to play with. Also, the lighting inside is the best I've ever seen in a fridge. With the glass shelves and bright light, nothing can hide or get lost. That can really help cut down on wasting food you have to toss because it was not seen or forgotten.

I've never had a french door fridge and this one also has the pull-out drawer. THAT is a really nice feature. Both the compartments and the temperature of the drawer are adjustable for whatever your needs. I still can't decide what I want to put in there but I know it'll be fun to figure out.

Freezer on the bottom is what you would expect. It does have a slide-out tray in the top of it that is good for pizzas, bacon, other flat frozen items. The drawer is deep but like any drawer freezer, things can get piled up and tossed around in there. Not as easy to find things in a drawer freezer than a side-by-side or top. But it suits it's purpose. Drawers glide very easily too.

CONS:
The ice and water system is the only thing I'm not thrilled about. It really needs a re-design and here's why. We're all familiar with how these things work. You push your glass against the concave paddle that cradles your glass and ice or water falls in. Simple. But LG had to try and fix it. And their fix needs fixing.

First, the paddles for water and ice are flat and are coated with the same slick paint as the doors. I know it sounds picky, but it takes some effort to hold the glass still while pressing these paddles because it slides around. For ice, this isn't that much of an issue because the ice area is 'in' the door and has the little tray/drip pan underneath.

But the water spout is in the worst place and is as poorly designed as it could be. It is not 'in' the door but is more even or flush with the front of the door but above and outside of the little niche where the glass is supposed to go. So if it drips after you fill your glass, it drips straight onto the fridge below or on to the floor. Moreover, the spout the water comes from is too short and angled in a way that makes it so you cannot put the lip of your glass under it. And if you use a Bubba 52 mug like me that's rounded, it's nearly impossible to fill without making a mess because the cup slides all over the place on the slick, flat paddle and you have to tilt it a bit so the water even gets in the cup. I can never get Bubba 52 completely filled.

Lastly, this fridge is very deep. It sticks out from my countertop at least 6-8 inches and my countertop is standard depth. A fridge this deep would look much better in a built-in section with sides and a top than just in a space at the end of a counter.

Hope those comments help.

title: VERY high quality stainless braid washer supply lines!
text:
As a person that has installed major appliances over 30 years, and worked with MANY braided water supply lines, I can tell you these 6' Sky Genius stainless braid hoses are extremely high-quality washer supply lines!

The 304 stainless braid has a very tight weave, and looks better than any braid I've seen. The nickel-plated brass connectors are precisely made, and they thread very easily onto the valves, and washer inlets.

By the heft and stiffness of the hoses, I believe these have a very sturdy core, unlike some that can kink fairly easily.

I put the angle connectors on my valves, because of the odd way the plumbing is in my garage. I have plenty of room behind the washer, but the angle connectors made the valve connections better than they were before, with the old straight rubber hoses (the old rubber hoses were in place when I moved into this house a couple years ago, and I hadn't gotten around to putting braided lines on yet).

I also love that these have red and blue striping to designate which one is hot and cold. Not all of them have that. So I view these Sky Genius no-burst washer supply lines as a very fine product, and at a super reasonable asking price!

Particularly, what goes into the water supply side of the solenoid valve, and what gets installed on the other side. However, our result is that our indoor humidity never gets above 27% in the winter when our new Aprilaire humidistat is set at a 35%. So we are not sure if the system is actually working long enough to effect anything. It could be that the indoor humidity remains the same as near outdoor ambient less the effect of heating inside air, although we hear the solenoid switched on and water running (from the return air duct on the first floor). The manuals need improvement, and that's why the videos are important. But I am entertained by what the video presenters leave out. Seems to be typical American speech that after one explains how to do it, they never say why - and we find that in our national news and some TED talks as well; the omissions/followups are just as important; so when you talk to your peer or teen, add a predicate to say why, and add safety and love as part of it as well. title: So far so good
text:
I got this on sale to prep for a baby. I live in a walk up apartment with no laundry.

Clothes came out very clean, smelling fresh. The spin cycle is awesome and removes a lot more water than by hand washing. If you have a lot of big heavy jeans or larger than queen sized sheets I wouldn't recommend but for leggings/sleepwear/bras/athletic clothing - this works great.

A few big notes:

1 I didn't hookup any water inlet since the hose does not fit any sink in my apt and I didn't want to risk messing with pipes in a rental. Dumping water in is a a bit of a chore and I only felt comfortable using it in the bathtub to avoid spilling when I dump the water in. If you can figure this out or have a hand spray in the shower it would be much easier.

2 There is no lint trap. I did one load with 2 towels and a bunch of lint came through the rinse cycle. I made a DIY trap by putting a sheer sock/stocking on the outlet tube and it works well. I would advise everyone to do this or your pipes will be clogged with lint.

3 Doing multiple loads can give off a rubbery odor, probably from the motor overworking. This makes me question how long this thing will last. I will update my review if anything happens.

text:
So first, I have replaced bearings on multiple front-load washers. Im not new at it, and my other replacements are still running strong.

So my old washer had the bearings go. So i took it apart and rebuilt it from the group up. New bearings, new spider arm, new screws, new shocks, new drain hose, pretty much every new part i could get. I was rebuilding this to send to my daughter for use in her new apartment, so i was replacing pretty much everything down to the door gasket.

So, everything goes smoothly. I disassemble, clean out all the TRASH from the old spider arm deteriorating, clean up the outer tubs and the basket really good, replace the bearings, and reassemble with new parts. Have the newly rebuilt washer and dryer delivered to my daughter.

It was late in the day when it was finally installed and she ran a few empty loads, looking for leaks (there was one, just from not tightening the clean-out door.. Oops, that was on me.

So, as she readied for bed, she tossed in a half load, just clothes for work the next day. As she laid down, a horrendous crashing came from the laundry room. When she went in, the washer was slamming against the wall with a horrendous grinding noise.

So, her proximity kept me from going there to evaluate myself, so i had a local repairman go take a look. Two things were wrong:

1) One of the 4 new shocks was completely blown, which was why the washer was hitting the wall. Not the fault of the bearings, and i just got done giving them a bad review as well.

2) The grinding noise was the brand new bearings. We went on facetime and she showed me how he checked the bearings, and i agreed with his assessment.

So yeah, first actual load on a brand new set of these and they died. Oh, this machine is an wf448aap/xaa which is in the compatibility chart. And the bearings i took out were exactly the same size and fit like a glove (again, not my first rodeo).

The guy wanted $450 just to replace the shocks, and probably double that for the bearings.

So, because of lousy parts, my $400 investment in the rebuild (plus my time) is out the window. I can buy her something BRAND NEW for less than the repair price.

Thanks for the lousy product, shows how quality is no longer a true goal for companies and how DIYers such as myself with the skills to commit projects can still lose their shirts due to bad craftsmanship of parts.

If you buy these parts, you're rolling the dice.

title: A new method of making an Aeropress hum
text:
My son turned me on to making a single serving of coffee with an Aeropress several years ago. While not as simple as plugging in a Keurig and pressing a button, the coffee that results is 10X better than the thin stuff than comes out of a K-machine.

Wait, make that 25X.

Aeropress is designed to use a small paper filter that is disposed after each use. They're not expensive, but can be a bit hard to find in the local stores. Amazon sells some reusable metal filters and they work well too. But along comes the Trobing Airflow Valve Filter system that combines a metal filter with a unique base that has a tiny opening for the brewed coffee to pour into your waiting cup.

That tiny opening is the difference between normal Aeropress coffee and this brew. It acts somewhat like an espresso machine in which coffee is forced under pressure through the grounds. And, somewhat like an espresso machine, you get some foam - almost crema - on the top of your coffee cup.

So does it work well?

Well, you're not going to think you just ordered an espresso at a coffee shop that uses an $8,000 La Marzocco espresso machine. But you will find a very nicely brewed cup of coffee that somehow tastes stronger than a cup brewed with stock Aeropress parts. The foam bubbles that the Trobing Airflow produces are larger than the tiny bubbles that make up true espresso crema, and they don't last as long either. But this device is really cool and makes great coffee.

A few watch-outs:

- first, read the directions! Trobing suggests pre-warming the Aeropress and your coffee cup with almost-boiling water. Do this! Then drain the Aeropress and add the coffee, then more almost-boiling water. And wait. Wait a bit more. It's worth it, even in a Keurig world. Then press that Aeropress plunger down and smell the difference between real coffee and fake machine coffee.

- second, the key to the Trobing is the tiny rubber valve in the center of the base. It comes out, and if you're not careful, it could disappear when you clean out the Aeropress after brewing. Trobing thoughfully includes a backup valve in the box, but lose both and you're back to using your stock Aeropress parts.

- last, the metal filter that Trobing uses only correctly fits into the base one way. If you can't easily lock the base of Trobing on the brew chamber of your Aeropress, then you have the filter in upside down. Flip it around and you'll know what I mean.

title: Works great, bolts right in, might have to cutout plug and reuse cord.
text:
The old ice maker ice cubes were melting together and there were icicles underneath the freeze tray.

Replaced the valve and shortened fill time without any change.

Found a YouTube video from Appliance Assistant on ice maker repair and trouble shooting. Using digital multimeter was able to determine using the test points behind the front cover that the motor was shot. So the heater stayed on because the motor could not push out the ice. So the water from the melting Ice cubes would then freeze together. The water from the melted ice cubes would create icicles.

Ordered this replacement ice maker from another site.

Was careful to go to Appliance sites to get the correct model number because there are several that are very similar. The model number for my refrigerator had a "Q" at the end. The same part number without the "Q" replacement is the RIM917. So make sure you order the correct model.

Had to use a razor knife to cut out a notch in the back to fit the fill tube adapter. There was a guideline molded into the plastic to follow.

The included cable was the wrong length, so had sto remove and reuse the cable from the old ice maker.

The cable holding clip does not hold the cable tightly even after trying to close it. Ended up using some Garden twist tie to secure the cable to the clip.

But other than these two inconveniences the replacement was fairly straightforward.

Did need a quarter inch ratchet drive, extension and socket to tighten the bottom bolt snug. Do not over tighten and strip the freezer tray boss.

The ice maker just made the first batch of ice and they are perfect. Took about 3 hours for the ice maker get cold enough to make its first batch.

Fortunately had also bought a new water supply line to replace the 12-year old one on the refrigerator. When we pulled the refrigerator out to unplug it the old line was just starting to leak and had a small puddle.

The old ice maker because the heater was going to constantly the Teflon coating was starting to flake off and peel.

Original equipment replacement units cost as much as $180 and around $120 on most appliance part sites. This one is less than half the cost. And behind the front cover it has all the same test points for ease of troubleshooting.

Because the fridge is 12 years old didn't want to spend too much.

The compressor was replaced under extended warranty with a top-of-the-line compressor because according to the technician that's all they had in stock... lucky for us!

With the money we saved between the ice maker and valve (both Supco), ordered a replacement bucket because our bucket is cracked along the guide rail.

According to the YouTube videos viewed ice makers today are only good for about 5 years. So if this one quits will just order this one again because the price is affordable and it does the job.

title: EZ-Cup vs. Solofill
text:
I bought both the EZ-Cup and the Solofill at a local Bed Bath and Beyond, though I may continue buying EZ-Cup filters at Amazon. Both work as advertised, and I would rate both of them with 4 stars. However there are some differences that make me choose the EZ-Cup over the Solofill most of the time I make coffee:

1. Filters make cleanup for the EZ-Cup easier and quicker, though Solofill is easier to fill because you don't have to monkey to around with a paper filter.
2. To me, the EZ-Cup filtered coffee tastes slightly smoother and has less sludge than Solofill.
3. Although you have to buy the EZ-Cup filters, it still works out to a lot less than buying K-Cups.
4. Solofill does brew much faster than EZ-Cup, about twice as fast. I think this is because the finer filtration with the EZ-Cup restricts the water flow more. However, the finer filtration is probably why the EZ-Cup coffee comes out slightly better. (See #2, above.)

So, as with most things, there are trade-offs for each good point about a product. If coffee quality and cleanup is more important to you, I would go with the EZ-Cup. If you like the idea of faster brew time, less environmental impact, and lower long term cost, then go with the Solofill.

title: Worked great!
text: I read a lot about people being disappointed after replacing their old seal with a generic seal like this one. There were may complaints that they did not seal well, or in many cases, hold the door shut properly. After installing this seal I would caution you that you will have that problem at first because the seal is shipped twisted into a figure 8 and folded in half. Once you remove the old seal and place the new seal on the door, there will be several areas that are crimped from the shipping and simply won't allow the door to seal to the refrigerator. I found that by holding the base of the seal steady against the door and pulling the top portion out in the crimped areas helped to get it back closer to the proper form. But to get it to seal properly and work as well as the original seal did, I placed a number of pencils in the pleat of the seal in all of the areas that were disformed from the shipping. It immediately sealed properly with the pencils in place, and after a week or two, I was able to remove the pencils without the seal loosing it's proper form. I hope this helps.

title: Great Washer/Dryer unit -EASY CONVERSION TO PROPANE-
text:
Not as noisy as i was expecting, and it washes very well!

Planning ahead and making sure you have hard floor or carpet furniture pads for the unit's feet will make it much easier moving around.

I converted this unit from Natural Gas to LP propane using the Kenmore 49572A Liquid Propane Conversion Kit also available on amazon. After watching some how-to videos on youtube and preparing myself for a full disassembly of the dryer unit I was pleasantly surprised to find that you can do the whole conversion just by removing the angled dryer plates just above the wash basin.

You will need a 1/2in FIP to Flare adapter for the gas connection in the back that you can pick up at any hardware store. As well as water lines, and a 1/2in yellow gas line, which ended up costing me an additional $50 or so for all.

Normally the delivery team will install for you, but at the time the connections were not ready.

So far this has been a great unit, would definitely recommend to anyone else in need of a propane powered clothes dryer!

Update sep 20 2018:

Ran into an issue with the unit giving me a "clear lint trap" error. My drier vent got partially obstructed so I thought that was the issue. Cleared the blockage and it would still give me the error and stop the unit. Would only run on air dry.

Did some googling and popped the rear access panel (2 screws) off that exposes the belt and motor and was able to access the Thermo sensor right off the fan. Took it out and tested the sensor with a volt meter. This sensor should read just above 50k ohms and mine was reading 51k so it seemed to be fine. Reinstalled and now its working fine. Ordered a new one just in case it really is bad. Likely just got quirky due to the partial obstruction.

https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B00DM8LUBK/ref=oh_aui_detailpage_o00_s00?ie=UTF8&psc=1

Really love how easily you can access these parts on the drier. Leaving it at 5 stars.

title: Small Wahing Machine for small places
text:
I purchased this to avoid having to go the laundromat and have been very pleased.

Good Things
-It's small and convenient
-It's light enough to move alone when empty
-It's surprisingly effective

Bad Things
-The "Lint Trap" isn't great. If you want to launder an item that has a large amount of lint and don't intend to run it through a dryer with a good lint filter then you should prepare to find another way to remove lint.

Other things
-A buzzer would be a nice addition to this unit.

Tips
-Find out how long it takes to fill your device with hot cold and warm water (yes, test each one individually. Odds are your flow rate is dependent on temperature of water). Use those times as a guidline for filling times so you do not have to watch it patiently.
-Weight matters more than size. Heavy items can weigh the agitator at the bottom down and if the clothes aren't spinning somewhat aggressively they wont get clean. If you are unsure of how much to load, fill the tub and add your soap and start the wash cycle. Keeping the lid open begin slowly feeding in clothing items one at a time allowing for the agitator to reverse directions and assuring that the clothes are still moving aggressively before each new addition. If the movement slows and doesn't return after 2 or 3 agitator reversals then you have put in too much and should take something out (you can pop it into the spin dryer tub while it waits)
-When the spin dryer is on the unit wobble a bit and can be noisy depending on the surface the unit is on. I have this unit on a metal shelf and have taken to keeping a folded towel underneath it to lessen noise and help prevent the unit from wandering when it wobbles.
-For people concerned about the size of the unit, some loads I wash often look like: My sheets (both fitted and flat) and pillowcases in one load; 3-4 pairs of khakis at once; 1-2 pairs of jeans at once ; 4-6 button down shirts at a time; 2-4 polos at once(weight dependent); 1-2 bath towels at once (if washing a bath sheet it can only handle one)

title: Great Dual Use Temperature/Humidity Controller
text:
I receive this item earlier this week and have been able to do some early testing. I found the interface to be relatively intuitive compared to some of the other temperature or humidity controllers on the market. The item functions as expected. The display is relatively bright and clear. Obviously the biggest benefit of this controller is that it controls both humidity and temperature while most other controllers available only control one or the other. Additionally, this item can either heat or cool using the temperature portion of the control and can also humidify or dehumidify with
the humidity portion of the control.

My only complaint is that the unit I received had the output connections mislabeled. The output electrical connections are suppose to be labeled "Work 1" and "Work 2", but mine were labeled "Heating" and "Cooling" which is obviously incorrect. An improvement would be to label the connections "Temperature" and "Humidity" to clarify what to plug into each port without referring to the directions. Even the correct labels aren't necessarily intuitive.

I use this controller to control temperature and humidity of a meat curing chamber, but could also be used for several other purposes.

text: This is the second Opal I have purchased.  We purchased the original Opal over 3 years ago and it worked great. It appears to get too cold and freezes, causing ice to get stuck in the thingy that pushes it out.  When this happens it makes a horrible screaming noise!  It literally sounds like two cats fighting and screaming in the alley, and it won’t stop.  I tried turning the power off, but, it just continues screaming!  You literally have to unplug the machine to make it stop!  To fix this I pour hot water into the water Reservoir and let it sit for a few minutes.  This melts whatever ice is clogging the machine.  I sent one back because of this and now the replacement is doing the same thing.  I guess it’s just a flaw in the machine.  It doesn’t defrost itself like the older version which is, what I believe, causes this issue.  I still highly recommend getting the older version or the newer version, However I would get the extended warranty on the new version, as I don’t know if this will limit the life of the machine.  They are great if you can tolerate two cats fight in the alley!  Good luck!

The repairman did come 2 days before Christmas, he replaced the control panel again. And he left, my daughter tested all the burners and guess what! 2 of the burners did NOT work! He was still in the driveway, so he came back in to check it. He said he reset the stove once again, all the burners came one. That afternoon, one of the two burners that had not worked then worked, only came on half way. The inner part of the burner was now dead. By the end of that day, that burner was totally dead. When i talked to LG a week before Christmas, LG said they would send my case in front of their review board and i would hear something with in 3-5 business days. It has been much longer then that, not including the holidays. Yes, i do have a partially working stove BUT that is NOT good enough! The repairman suggested me to that Lg should buy my stove back seeings how this last repair did not work. I happen to agree!

My husband bought this stove for me on Feb 14th, i was thrilled! I love to bake and cook and even canning. I had the stove for less then a month and the large right burner died. I called to have it repaired. We kept using the stove, and before the repairman could get to us, the entire top of dead! You could push the buttons, they would come on but didn't heat up. The repairman came out, looked at the stove and said he had to order the parts. Two weeks later, he replaced the mother board and everything was up and running just fine. Two months later, we had the same issue. The left burner goes this time. Again, the same repairman comes out looks at the stove, he again orders the same parts. He replaces the mother board again. On the 3rd repair, LG tells me the repair guy is the one who has to call it a lemon, the repair guy tells me its LG that has to call it a lemon. OK, so he repaired it and i just let it go, WHICH i have NOT have! Dec 14 we call the repairman again, I am now on my 4th repair for the same thing! Now LG wants to see my receipt for the stove, and they are sending it to their claims dept to see if they can replace this stupid stove. I really hope they do NOT plan to send me another stove like this one!) Last week, the repairman came out, of course they have to order the parts and i am just betting, my stove will NOT be repaired in time for me to cook the family Christmas dinner!

title: Be careful with the thermostat!
text:
This replaced the heating element and thermostat on my 25 year old Kenmore dryer. Both fit, and looked almost identical to the originals. However, be really careful installing the thermostat. The one I received did not quite fit and I had to bend it to get it onto the terminal. When I did so, it broke (where the two dissimilar metals are joined). I was able to solder it back together, and also decided that bending down the flange where the prong on the dryer fits into the hole also helps. Anyway, after soldering and doing that bent flange, I was able to get it on without breaking it.
Also note that even installing these two items may not be enough. My dryer still did not heat with the new elements. I spent some time reading the owners manual and was able to find a hint that the high heat shut-off fuse will blow if the dryer overheats. This needs to be replaced if it blows. So I had to order one of these. After I installed it (very easy!), the dryer worked fine. It is quite possible that I only needed to replace this part, and not the element, so could have saved myself $35 if I had done so. I recommend replacing this fuse first to see if that restores the heating capability of your dryer.

title: Not for snowbirds. Requires too much bandwidth. Poor support.
text:
I really wanted this to work. It was easy to set up. I had no problem registering at the web site and setting up triggers. It was easy to go view sensor history, etc. on the web site. But triggering of emails and texts did not work. It is supposed to contact you when the temperature range is exceeded.

I reported this and 2 days later got an automated response telling me the problem report was being closed. So I submitted the bug report again. 2 days later it was automatically closed again. I did call and talked to someone in support, who promised me that they would determine the problem and would keep the bug report open.

After another email exchange with tech support a month later, and with no resolution to the lack of triggered alerts, I gave up. But I could still go to the web site daily and check status -- which was great, though not optimal.

Then, I reduced my Time Warner Internet service to a maintenance level (aka "Everyday Low Price") for the season and suddenly everything stopped working. AcuRite pointed at TW as the culprit, claiming insufficient bandwidth. TW claimed that they could ping my modem and I was getting the required 1 Mb of upload speed, but I was no longer there to verify it.

The upshot is that I'd have to pay $50 a month to TW to get more than 1 Mb of upload bandwidth to make this work. I could get a security service for less than that. So the great experiment failed.

I'm now trying the MarCell product, which is cellular based, rather than internet based. So far so good, but it requires $100 per year for cell service -- not ideal, but cheaper than $50 per month for Internet.

The Kenmore simply wasn't worth repairing, so we opted to purchase this unit based on looks alone, since we were without a working unit for a month and were getting desperate at that point.

I opted for the 5 year service plan through the seller (not Amazon), so I am not too worried about major repairs in that period.

If I had to do it again, I would do a bit more research.

It is several inches smaller in the loading area than the device it replaced, which must be due to the quality of the build and the sound insulation. Secondly, it lacks a delayed start option. I assumed that a unit at this price point would have that feature since I've seen it on so many other less expensive models and brands.

That is an important feature to me (cost and convenience, not because of noise, this thing is quiet as a mouse) and if it's important to you, look elsewhere for another product.

Just put it in a suitable tray, pour 1 part of household vinegar and one part of hot water over it, flatten with dead weight to fully submerge, wait for the reaction to be over (no gas bubbles anymore), rinse with fresh water, and put it back. title: Perfect greasy restaurant tech for home but terrible to install
text:
I had three generations of microwave hood in the house and always know that it is a very bad idea if you do any stir fry. And I do it every day. Last time when the microwave broke these hoods with well over 400 CFM (typical of microwave hoods) cost over $1000. Now if you add the price of this and a counter top microwave, it's the same as a 400 CFM microwave hood I had years ago.

Microwave hoods are flush with the 12" deep cabinet but I stir fry in the front stoves because of the large wok, so the smoke goes straight to the ceiling. Range hoods have a roof extruding out to catch the smoke.

Grease will be collected in the hood and will drip somewhere. In my microwave hoods grease were everywhere, getting out from the door latch holes, or from the control panel seams. The last one is the worst, grease drips from the ceiling vent inside the cooking chamber and into the food down there. There's no way you can clean it without dissembling the microwave.

In this hood there's an easily removable oil tunnel to collect grease. There's a round tunnel circling each fan to collect grease falling onto the fan wall by centrifugal force. There are tubes to connect the circular tunnel to the removable oil tunnel at the bottom of the hood. All you need to do is occasionally pull it out and rinse it.

The hood comes in with a few dings at the top that will be covered by the cabinet after installation. Am I lucky? Some foam padding is broken inside. But I believe the packaging and delivery is not bad at all, relatively. You cannot believe how may broken things I have received lately across the board.

The hood seems to be well made. It looked like a twin turbo jet engine inside a strong, brushed stainless steel box. The box is precise, no sign of welding, more like a plastic mold with abrupt or gentle edges at will.

I do not know if it's over 900 CFM. But even for 400 CFM, the same as my microwave, it will be infinitely better because the air have to go through an obstacle course before getting into the vent. For the reviewer who said it's struggling to keep a tissue up, I tried with 4 typical kitchen paper towel stacked together as one and somehow they stay right there on the grease filter. Noise is irrelevant as I can only hear the air hitting hard on the vent above. From the sound of it I can say it's much more powerful than my microwave hoods.

The touch controls WERE the way to go. Many years ago touch buttons with absolutely no movements began to appear on fans and light switches. But then they were never really popular. Until those cheap rubber membrane buttons conquered the world. They are cheap and provide feedback but it's mad to put them on range stoves. The heat created all sorts of problems. I'm living with it now as I have to replace the whole panel costing a few hundred dollars at least. And I didn't bother to repair the leak in my stainless steel dishwasher because only the on off button works, remembering the last favorite cycle. I throw it away and got a plastic one. These membrane like buttons are only good for electronics, where a few years is like eternity.

The manual is not bad at all, language is perfect. But the content can be improved. The "original" state means the off state when the power button is red and most buttons are dimmed. Is it difficult to say that? The standby state means all buttons are functioning and most of them are white. To turn the fan on you need two button pushes - one for entering standby (or you can say power on), and another one to start the fan. The hood will return to "off" mode if idle for a long time. That's a little inconvenience to save the standby current and to save the world.

The heat sensor button and auto mode mentioned in the manual doesn't work. Perhaps not for this model. And it's not described in the listing, fair enough.

It's a lot lighter than a micorwave hood, with equally distributed weight that one person can easily lift it. But it's much more difficult to install than a microwave hood, professional or DIY. You have to consider that before buying this excellent product.

If you make it easier to install like a microwave hood, you can just add $100 to the price. Nobody will bother to turn up to install it for you for $40 here. Only if you are in good terms with a handyman and it happens you are on his route that day. It cost me $90 to clear the kitchen drain outside the house for an unlicensed retired fireman. Then I found out 20 years ago that it will clear if I pour one or two full bottle of strong acid drain openers. And if I don't install a grease trap, it will clog regularly. A mains pressure regulator for living on the hills? A quote over $1000 !

My 3 generation of micowave hoods all uses the same old vent pipe setup, where the ceiling vent is about at the middle of the cabinet. The vent outlet of this hood is close to the front of the cabinet. So you may have a problem of alignment. Flexible duct is not the recommended solution. Noisy (?) and collect grease. I got a rigid but adjustable 90 deg elbow. First align the dotted joints together to give a straight one. Twist the 1st section to give the maximum of 22.5 deg. Twist the next section to give 22.5 deg in the opposite. Then you have a upright vent with a little offset. Since you need a reducer, there's little room to maneuver. You have to sort out the vent first before installing the hood. I sort of followed the instruction doing the vent last, so I ended up doing it all over again. 8" is the industry recommended duct size for 900 CFM. I have 7" that will do but six and four is definitely on the small side. If you need to cut vent, I suggest oscillator tool with metal blade. You will find use for them. It's noisy but won't take long.

First, there's no bracket to help you hang the hood on the wall so you can proceed to secure it. There's a pair of brackets but it's either wall mount, OR top mount. If you want top mount, the brackets get in the way. Then there's no template for the screws. The mounting hardware is of good quality. How much does a piece of paper cost? And you can at least jack up the price by $10 if you have a template. The dimensional drawings are very good but I don't want to do a simple technical drawing on my greasy cabinet bottom. And I don't have something 30" wide that I can draw on.

Now if you have a modular cabinet, that each cabinet have it's own walls when you split them apart, the screws are supposed to go up on the vertical side walls. You can't use any other methods like nuts and bolts, toggle bolts, by drilling holes at the cabinet bottom. You have to destroy part of the side walls and still the rest of the wall will get in the way.

The keyhole shape of the mounting holes suggests that you can put in the screws half way in first, lift the hood and let the screw head go through the hole, then push the hood towards the wall to hang it. Finally, tighten the screws from inside the hood. The problem is, the screw head matches closely the bigger end of the mounting hole. The screw positions have to be precise.

Assume you have the screws in almost perfect position, you still need a two person crew to lift the hood, eyeball the screws so that all four of them goes through the mounting hole at the same time. That's why you can't just hire a crew to travel 20 odd miles just to install a few screws for $40. If they don't do templates than it's a 3 person crew to mark the positions while the hood is lifted in place.

And that's not the end of the story. I doubt if you can use a screw driver vertically to tighten the screws from under the hood, not even a very long driver. That also eliminates the possibility of using power tools. A short driver may go in but can tighten at most two of the screws. So I have to bring out my snake driver part that I never used for about 2 decades. It works but first you have to use power tools to tighten and loosen the screws without the hood to make sure the screws can be tightened by hand via a snake in the final step. The pilot hole was narrow because the screw have to hang the hood upside down. So it's tough to drive the screws in by hand.

The screws are of good quality but given half the chance, a power driver will grind off the screw head instead of driving it. I ruined 3.5 of the 7 screws that I received.

The 2nd time I installed it, I figured out how to do it by myself. Use two c-clamps on the cabinet side walls. It's only the sides are in contact but if yours are really expensive, you can pad the clamps, protect it the way you want. They will hold the hood with the back leaning against the back wall. You can slip in the hood close to the bottom of the cabinet above so you can put the long screw into the predrilled holes and start tightening.

The 1st time I installed it with a two person team, we managed to lift the hood into the half way in screws. All four of them and it's a miracle for me. I was thinking of 2 to 3 screws and then figuring out how to get the rest in position. So I share with you how I make templates without big papers and not even a triangle or t-square. First cut small triangle piece of papers as pointers to critical points on the top of hood, like the screw positions, cord hole position, the corners and the edges of the hood. Then use a paper hole punch to make a hole in the middle of the triangle. Use a small piece of painter's tape to secure the triangle to the top of hood via the hole. You can easily take out the paper that way. When all triangles are in place, put small amount of school glue on them. Then put papers on top to connect the triangles. Align straight paper edges with edges of the hood. In the end you will have a single piece of multilayered template with all the right markings. Then you use double sided glue pads to stick it to the cabinet bottom. A crafty method that you can get all supplies in Joann.

title: It is a pain to clean/messy especially if not installed in an accessible location
text:
Pros:
1) Easy to install
2) Redirects heat/humidity into the house
3) Not expensive

Cons:
1) The filter is not very fine so dryer dust blows everywhere. Attaching pantyhose to the front of teh filter helps reduce dust but not 100%, so you will have fine dust everywhere.
2) The zip ties barely hold the thing to the vent tube so if you don't tape it with duct tape, it will fall off every time you touch it and you will go crazy. (but duct tape works fine).
3) You have to clean the filter pretty much every load, so if you installed it up high or behind the drier or in some other inconvenient place you will be kicking yourself. It is not hard to remove and clean the filer (after duct taping it together, or course), but if you installed it out of the way it will be a pain.

Overall: YOU GET WHAT YOU PAY FOR. This works with some MacGyver fixes, but if you don't like fiddling with things or you don't have an accessible place to install it then you probably should look elsewhere.
